A server component's code — its imports, its logic, any heavy dependencies it pulls in — never becomes part of the client JavaScript bundle at all. It runs once on the server, produces a description of UI (not HTML, and not JSX — a special serialized format), and that description streams to the client alongside whatever client components are interspersed in the tree.

Hydration is the process, mentioned above, of React attaching event listeners and internal state to already-rendered server HTML rather than re-creating DOM nodes from scratch. A subtle but important consequence:

Props passed from a server component to a client component must be serializable

A hydration mismatch doesn't just log a warning and move on cleanly

— React discards and re-renders the mismatched DOM subtree client-side, which means any perceived SSR performance benefit for that specific section is lost, and in some cases visible content can flicker or shift as the corrected client-rendered version replaces the server-rendered one.
